name: Bone-setting

card.summary: A traditional hands-on practice of manipulating joints and setting fractures, sometimes sought by people who want better posture, spinal alignment and a straighter-standing frame.
card.aka: Traditional bone setting, bonesetting, die-da (China), sekkotsu (Japan)
card.note: Studies of traditional bone setters for fractures in low- and middle-income countries report serious complications, including limb loss.

quick.overview:
Bone-setting is a folk medicine tradition in which a practitioner uses their hands to reduce dislocations, realign joints and set broken bones. It exists in many cultures and predates modern orthopedics, physiotherapy and chiropractic. In appearance terms, people who seek it out are usually after better posture, a straighter spine and relief from neck or back stiffness, all of which change how tall and upright someone stands.

Research is a mix of small randomized trials on neck and back pain (mostly from Finland, where a folk bone-setting tradition was studied) and a larger body of observational reviews of traditional bone setters treating fractures in countries such as Nigeria. The first group compared bone-setting with physiotherapy or exercise; the second documents a notable rate of complications.
quick.how: A practitioner, often trained by family apprenticeship rather than formal schooling, handles the affected joint or limb with manipulation, traction, massage, splints or herbal preparations, depending on the tradition. In the Finnish trials, a course was a series of weekly sessions with experienced folk healers. People interested in posture and frame generally approach it as manual treatment for a stiff neck, back or shoulder rather than as a cosmetic procedure.
quick.risks: Reviews of traditional bone setters in low- and middle-income countries describe limb- and life-threatening complications after fracture treatment, including gangrene, and report that many patients later need orthodox surgical care. Spinal and neck manipulation by any practitioner carries its own known risks. Orthopedic surgeons generally advise having fractures and dislocations assessed in a hospital.

lead: Bone-setting is a traditional practice in which practitioners manipulate joints, reduce dislocations and set fractures by hand. Versions of it exist worldwide, and it predates the formal professions of surgery, physiotherapy and chiropractic. [1]

For appearance, the link runs through posture and frame: people who feel their neck, shoulders or back are stiff or out of line sometimes seek a bone-setter, with the aim of standing straighter and moving more freely. The practice is not a cosmetic procedure and is not usually marketed as one.

Randomized trials have compared folk bone-setting with physiotherapy or light exercise for prolonged neck and low-back pain [3][4][5][6], while reviews of traditional bone setters in Nigeria and other low- and middle-income countries have documented serious complications in fracture care [7][8].

chain: Hands-on manipulation of stiff or misaligned joints
Possible relief of neck and back pain and stiffness
Easier upright posture and a straighter-looking frame
angle.text: People seek bone-setters for stiff necks, backs and joints, and a freer, more upright posture changes how tall and balanced someone looks. Appearance is a by-product of treating a musculoskeletal complaint, not the stated aim of the practice.

infobox: Egyptian papyrus describing bone injury care, c. 1552 BC [1]

paras: Bone-setters treat injuries to bones and joints by hand: re-aligning dislocated joints, setting fractures, and manipulating stiff or painful areas. Methods vary with region and may include traction, massage, splinting with wood or bamboo, and herbal poultices. [1][7]

In China the tradition is associated with martial artists and is called die-da, and it overlaps with tuina manipulation [1][2]. Japan has sekkotsu, and India has the haad vaidya tradition [1]. A review of traditional medicinal plants notes that herbal preparations have long been used for swelling, pain and fracture recovery in bone-setting practice. [9]

Records of splinting and casting bone injuries appear in the Edwin Smith Papyrus from Ancient Egypt, dated to about 1552 BC. In the British Isles, bone-setting skill was often passed down in families (such as the Taylors, Thomases and Matthews), and after the dissolution of the monasteries in the 16th century some former monks and nuns with medical knowledge became bone-setters. [1]

Eighteenth-century figures such as Sally Mapp, who treated dislocations in London and Epsom and died in 1737, were widely known, though contemporaries divided over whether bone-setters were skilled healers or quacks. [1] Medical journals of the 19th century, including the British Medical Journal in 1888, were already discussing bone-setting and its relationship to orthodox surgery. [10]

In parts of Africa and Asia, where orthopedic specialists are scarce, traditional bone setters remain a first point of care for fractures and dislocations and attract large numbers of patients. A review of practice in Nigeria found that the tradition is transmitted from one generation to the next and has no formal training. [7] Studies of why people use them in Ilorin, Nigeria, examine cost, access and cultural trust. [11]
Where bone setters have been offered training, reviewers report improvements in their performance, and recent studies describe bone setters as willing to cooperate with orthodox services. [7][8][12]

A Finnish randomized trial with blinded outcome assessment enrolled 42 working-age adults with prolonged neck pain and compared five weekly sessions of bone-setting by experienced folk healers with a comparison treatment, with one-year follow-up. [3] A second randomized trial examined traditional bone-setting in chronic neck pain. [4]

For back pain, a randomized trial in 132 eligible patients compared traditional bone-setting, light exercise therapy and physiotherapy with a six-month follow-up. [5] A long-term follow-up trial compared the same three approaches. [6] A randomized pilot trial studied bone-setting for chronic low back pain, and a surface-EMG study compared back-muscle activity before and after bone-setting and conventional physical therapy. [13][14]

Observational research focuses on fracture care. A 2023 systematic review of 12 observational studies from low- and middle-income countries, covering 833 participants, counted 691 complications of treatment by traditional bone setters, including limb- and life-threatening events and deaths, while noting that bone setters were keen to work with orthodox services. [8] A review of Nigerian practice reported gangrene of the extremities as the most serious problem. [7]

Related traditions have also been studied: a 2020 meta-analysis of nine randomized trials found low-quality evidence that tuina, a Chinese bone-setting manipulation, had a higher effectiveness rate than massage or cervical traction for cervical vertigo. [2] None of these studies measured appearance outcomes.

Reviews describe delayed presentation to hospitals, poorly reduced or infected fractures, tight splinting that cuts off circulation and can lead to gangrene and amputation, and in some series deaths. [7][8] The authors of these reviews typically recommend training and integration with orthodox care rather than abandoning the tradition outright. [7][8]
A review of traditional medicine in Nigeria likewise weighs its cultural relevance and accessibility against delayed conventional treatment and the risks of unregulated remedies. [15]

timeline.event: The Edwin Smith Papyrus describes Egyptian care of bone injuries with splints and casts. [1]
After the dissolution of the monasteries in the British Isles, some former monks and nuns with medical knowledge become bone-setters; family lines such as the Taylors persist for generations. [1]
Sally Mapp, a well-known London bone-setter, dies. [1]
The Apothecaries Act in Britain changes surgeon training and lets some bone-setters enter the profession. [1]
The British Medical Journal publishes an article titled 'On Bone-Setting'. [10]
A Finnish randomized trial compares traditional bone-setting, light exercise and physiotherapy for prolonged back pain. [5]
A systematic review of 12 studies catalogs complications of traditional bone setting in low- and middle-income countries. [8]
